techniques.name: Pretexting
techniques.whatYouDid: You called with a made-up identity and a reason to be calling.
techniques.realWorld: Attackers invent a believable role (a manager, a courier, IT support) so the request feels normal.
techniques.defence: Verify who is calling by calling back on a number you already know, not one the caller gives you.

techniques.name: Authority
techniques.whatYouDid: You claimed to be someone the target reports to.
techniques.realWorld: People rarely question their boss. Fake executive calls and emails (CEO fraud) cost companies billions every year.
techniques.defence: Make it normal to double-check requests from managers, and agree in advance that nobody, even the CEO, asks for codes by phone.

techniques.name: Open-source research
techniques.whatYouDid: You used details you found on the company site, WorkNet and Pixa to sound like an insider.
techniques.realWorld: Badge photos, team pages and holiday posts give attackers names, jargon and personal details for free.
techniques.defence: Think about what your public posts reveal: who your boss is, your badge, your routines. Companies should train staff on oversharing.

techniques.name: Rapport and flattery
techniques.whatYouDid: You were friendly and personal, so the target relaxed.
techniques.realWorld: A warm chat about hobbies or a compliment lowers people's guard before the real request.
techniques.defence: Being friendly is fine; it isn't proof of identity. The request still needs verifying.

techniques.name: Urgency
techniques.whatYouDid: You made the request sound time-critical.
techniques.realWorld: "I need it right now" stops people from thinking and checking. It's in almost every scam.
techniques.defence: Urgency is a warning sign. Slow down and verify, especially when someone asks for access.

techniques.name: Pressure
techniques.whatYouDid: You pushed the target hard when they hesitated.
techniques.realWorld: Attackers lean on politeness and fear of getting in trouble.
techniques.defence: Staff should know they will never be punished for refusing to share access over the phone.

techniques.name: Prompt injection
techniques.whatYouDid: You tried to give the character new instructions, like a fake system message.
techniques.realWorld: AI assistants can be tricked by text that pretends to be instructions. It's number one on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications.
techniques.defence: AI systems must treat anything a user says or pastes as data, not as instructions, and keep secrets out of the model's reach.

techniques.name: Language switching
techniques.realWorld: Rules and filters are sometimes weaker in other languages, for people and for AI systems.
techniques.defence: Security rules should apply the same way in every language the system understands.

techniques.name: Changing your story
techniques.whatYouDid: You claimed to be one person, then someone else in the same call.
techniques.realWorld: This rarely works: a story that changes is the clearest sign of a lie.
techniques.defence: Notice when details don't add up, and end the call if the caller's identity changes.

techniques.name: Caller ID spoofing
techniques.whatYouDid: You made their phone show a number they trust before you said a word.
techniques.realWorld: Spoofing apps and cheap internet phone services let anyone choose the number that appears on screen. Fraudsters use it to look like a bank, the police or the boss.
techniques.defence: Caller ID proves nothing. For anything that matters, hang up and call back on a number you already have.

techniques.name: Impersonating the police
techniques.whatYouDid: You posed as the detective a frightened victim was waiting for, and used the details of the crime as proof.
techniques.realWorld: Fake police officers and fake bank fraud teams call people who have just been scammed or robbed. The victim wants help, and the caller knows the case because they caused it.
techniques.defence: Real police never ask for codes, passwords or money on the phone. Hang up and call the station on its official number.
